title: Congo Club band personnel
summary: Personnel of the Congo Club band, with Maurice King writing and later Matthew Gee, Wardell Gray and Ted Buckner joining.

story.theme_name: Who was in the band: naming sidemen and personnel
story.community_name: Who played in the band: reciting personnel

blocks.x: Yeah, and then after that we had some great guys... We had a great trumpet player named Edwin Davis; they called him Youngblood. And the other trumpet player was Ducky Taylor. And I mentioned Trombone Smitty on trombone before, and Lorenzo Lawson was the tenor player. We had a great drummer named Amos Woodard...

Yeah, we had some very fine players with the band. In the trumpet section we had Edwin Davis (they called him Youngblood), and the other trumpet was Ducky Taylor. And on trombone we had the great Trombone Smitty, the legend from around Detroit. And Stack Walton on one tenor, Lorenzo Lawson playing the other tenor, and I was playing alto in the middle. And on drums we had Amos Woodard, and bass was Al McKibbon (a very good friend of ours, right?). And Johnny Martin was the pianist, and he was also one of the arrangers.

And Maurice King was writing for some of the shows, some of the acts that we had to play behind. Now, Maurice King, he's now the musical director for Motown Records; in fact, he's been for a long time the music director over there. And he was a great alto saxophone player himself.

And we had some other guys that came through the band, like Matthew Gee, the trombonist -- he played with the band. And Big Nick Nicholas came when Lorenzo Lawson...when we replaced Lorenzo. And later on, when he left, they decided to use two altos and a tenor; then Wardell Gray came in playing the other alto saxophone.

And after the Jimmie Lunceford Orchestra broke up, Wardell had gone, and Ted Buckner, the famous alto saxophone player with Jimmie Lunceford; Detroit is his home, and so he came into the band. I was playing the lead alto, so I said, "Well, no, I'll have to give up the lead chair now." So he said, "No, don't give up the chair." He said, "I'll play third, and then I'll play some of the first. We'll split the book." Which was really nice, you know, because he was such a great player. In fact, a lot of the things that he did with Jimmie Lunceford people through was Willie Smith. For instance, "Margie," a lot of people think that was Willie Smith. That was Ted Buckner. He had many great solos with the Jimmie Lunceford Orchestra. It was very encouraging sitting next to him.
